MetaCheck Report

Image size effect on memory generalizes to deeper encoding and cannot be explained by perceptual measures

2026-11-11 · Metacheck 0.4.3.27

3to fix3to check0to decide by hand2fine8not applicable

To fix (3)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 3 imprecise p values out of 50 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p-value ≤ 0.05 Repeated measures ANOVAs were performed using the R anova_test and get_anova_table functions where get_anova_table automatically applies the Greenhouse-Geisser sphericity correction only to factors violating the sphericity assumption (i.e., Mauchly’s test significant p-value ≤ 0.05).
p’s ≥ 0.85 No interaction between encoding task and image size on memory measures was found (all F’s < 2, all p’s ≥ 0.85, all ŋG2 ≤ 0.005).
p’s > .05 Additional analyses revealed that RT was influenced by encoding task (H(2) = 7.54, p = .023, but no post-hoc comparisons survived the stringent Bonferroni-Dunn correction with all p’s > .05, see Fig. 3F), and that image memorability was consistent across encoding tasks (see osf.io/kbmr9/).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 328 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 1 codebook/README/label source and 328 data columns across 7 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

To fix Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 5 files: 3 data, 2 documentation.
  • We found 3 tabular data files and extracted 328 columns from 3 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 1 study group (ex5), plus 1 collection-level file (README/ro-crate metadata). We ran automated data-quality checks on 328 columns; 289 columns have at least one potential issue (289 columns with numeric values stored as text). 3 of 3 spreadsheet files have at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

To check (3)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 8 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = 0.125 We also found a significant effect of encoding task on accuracy of already-seen images and on decision criterion (but not on dprime) and these reflected significant increased accuracy and reduced criterion for perceptual encoding relative to both naturalistic or intentional memorization encoding experiments (accuracy: F(2, 167) = 8.42, p = 3.27*10 -4, ŋG2 = 0.072; criterion: F(2, 167) = 3.53, p = .031, ŋG2 = 0.038; dprime: F(2, 167) = 2.10, p = 0.125, ŋG2 = 0.022; see Table 2 for details).
p’s ≥ 0.85 No interaction between encoding task and image size on memory measures was found (all F’s < 2, all p’s ≥ 0.85, all ŋG2 ≤ 0.005).
p = 0.154 Examining signal detection theory measures, memory sensitivity (dprime) was not significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 1.893, p = 0.154, ŋG2 = 0.022) although there was a gradual increase in the mean memory sensitivity from lowest in naturalistic encoding to highest in perceptual encoding.
p = 0.053 AUC was not significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 2.988, p = 0.053, ŋG2 = 0.035) although mean AUC increased with encoding task in the same manner as memory sensitivity (dprime), and as can be seen in Figure 3E, AUC was significantly correlated with dprime in each of the experiments (naturalistic encoding experiment: r = 0.92, t(56) = 16.9, p = 1.0510 -23 ; intentional memorization encoding experiment: r = 0.93, t(65) = 21.0, p = 1.2810 -30 ; perceptual encoding experiment: r = 0.98, t(43) = 33.90, p = 1.17*10 -32 ).
p’s > .05 Additional analyses revealed that RT was influenced by encoding task (H(2) = 7.54, p = .023, but no post-hoc comparisons survived the stringent Bonferroni-Dunn correction with all p’s > .05, see Fig. 3F), and that image memorability was consistent across encoding tasks (see osf.io/kbmr9/).

To check Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests

What we found

We found 19 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

Show details

We recommend checking the sentences below, and add any missing effect sizes.

For t-tests with a reported d, coherence checks yielded 3 indeterminate cases.

For F-tests with a reported eta-squared effect size, coherence checks yielded 1 indeterminate case.
We found an effect of image size on perception (F(3,132) = 12.8, p = 2.15*10 -7, ŋG2 = 0.060, 3° better than 6°: p = 0.00075, 6° similar to 12°: p = 1 and 12° lower than 15.5°: p = 0.011).
There was also an effect of category-related task on perception (F(1,44) = 71.04, p = 9.8610 -11, ŋG2 = 0.193) reflecting slightly higher performance on the person-related question (in red in Figure 2A) than on the place-related question (in blue in Figure 2A, p = 1.7410 -15 ).
An interaction between image size and category-related task on perception was found (F(3,132) = 21.87, p = 1.46*10 -11, ŋG2 = 0.121) and it likely reflected a small drop in performance in the person-related question in the 12° sized images, while for the place-related question there was a small drop of performance in the 6° sized images.
We also found a significant effect of encoding task on accuracy of already-seen images and on decision criterion (but not on dprime) and these reflected significant increased accuracy and reduced criterion for perceptual encoding relative to both naturalistic or intentional memorization encoding experiments (accuracy: F(2, 167) = 8.42, p = 3.27*10 -4, ŋG2 = 0.072; criterion: F(2, 167) = 3.53, p = .031, ŋG2 = 0.038; dprime: F(2, 167) = 2.10, p = 0.125, ŋG2 = 0.022; see Table 2 for details).
We also found a significant effect of encoding task on accuracy of already-seen images and on decision criterion (but not on dprime) and these reflected significant increased accuracy and reduced criterion for perceptual encoding relative to both naturalistic or intentional memorization encoding experiments (accuracy: F(2, 167) = 8.42, p = 3.27*10 -4, ŋG2 = 0.072; criterion: F(2, 167) = 3.53, p = .031, ŋG2 = 0.038; dprime: F(2, 167) = 2.10, p = 0.125, ŋG2 = 0.022; see Table 2 for details).
We also found a significant effect of encoding task on accuracy of already-seen images and on decision criterion (but not on dprime) and these reflected significant increased accuracy and reduced criterion for perceptual encoding relative to both naturalistic or intentional memorization encoding experiments (accuracy: F(2, 167) = 8.42, p = 3.27*10 -4, ŋG2 = 0.072; criterion: F(2, 167) = 3.53, p = .031, ŋG2 = 0.038; dprime: F(2, 167) = 2.10, p = 0.125, ŋG2 = 0.022; see Table 2 for details).
As was evident in the 2-way ANOVA analyses (see above), when examining only the effect of encoding task on overall memory, accuracy for already seen images was significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 8.424, p = 0.000327, ŋG2 = 0.092; 1-way ANOVA) with higher overall accuracy in the perceptual encoding experiment relative to the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 0.000442) but no difference between the accuracy in the intentional memorization encoding experiment and that of the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 1).
Examining signal detection theory measures, memory sensitivity (dprime) was not significantly affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 1.893, p = 0.154, ŋG2 = 0.022) although there was a gradual increase in the mean memory sensitivity from lowest in naturalistic encoding to highest in perceptual encoding.
Decision criterion was, however, affected by encoding task (F(2,167) = 3.461, p = 0.034, ŋG2 = 0.04) with lower overall criterion in the perceptual encoding experiment relative to the intentional memorization encoding experiment (p = 0.0479) but no difference between the decision criterion in the intentional memorization encoding experiment and that in the naturalistic encoding experiment (p = 1).
First, we found that in each experiment the overall dprime was significantly above chance (i.e. 1-sampled t-tests for dprime above 0 (naturalistic encoding experiment: M = 0.85, 95% confidence interval [0.67, 1.04], t(57) = 9.25, p = 6.04610 -13 ; intentional memorization encoding experiment: M = 1.00, 95% confidence interval [0.81, 1.19], t(66) = 10.56, p = 8.15910 -16 ; perceptual encoding experiment: M = 1.18, 95% confidence interval [0.85, 1.52], t(44) = 7.07, p = 9.044*10 -9 ).

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Participants were recruited via Prolific online platform (https://www.prolific.co/) with the following recruitment criteria: age (18-35 years old), fluency in English, credible participation experience on Prolific (at least 200 runs and acceptance rate of 98% and above), and participation with a desktop computer/laptop (not handheld devices).

Each participant participated only once to ensure she/he were naïve to the study’s memory aspects (for additional performance-based exclusion criteria see Analyses below).

While recruitment criteria and participant demographics were available via Prolific, the participants’ identity was completely anonymized and we were blind to any identifying details (each participant was known by her/his Prolific-encrypted alphanumeric string).

Demographic data from Prolific was missing for one participant from the intentional memorization encoding experiment and for three participants from the naturalistic encoding experiment.

Prior to their participation participants were provided with an overall overview of the experiment as is common on Prolific.

All participants were paid at the end of their participation according to the criteria set by Prolific (regardless of their level of performance) and this was performed via the Prolific interface.

Participants were first presented with a demographics questionnaire (age range, gender, handedness, vision, and highest level of education).

The experiment started with the exposure phase where participants were asked to observe each image that appeared on the screen and follow any instructions that may appear (without any information about the memory aspect of the experiment that were to follow later).

During the exposure phase, 4 unexpected attention checks appeared (after every 32 images) where participants were asked to press the spacebar as fast as they could in order to continue the experiment (a black screen with the instructions “Press SPACE as fast as you can” appeared).

Participants were presented with surprise old-new recognition memory test instructions (to press leftward arrow if they recall seeing the image earlier or rightward arrow if not) and asked to press the shift key to proceed.

The experiment ended with an end of experiment screen and participants were then redirected back to Prolific with a completion code.

The procedures of this experiment were precisely as those of the naturalistic encoding experiment except for the instructions before the exposure phase where participants were asked to memorize the images they were about to see (see Fig. 1A).

Second, after each image presentation (2s, as in the other experiments), participants were presented with two image-content related sequential questions.

The participants were required to answer with no time restrictions.

  1. Test phase: after the exposure phase participants were given an old/new recognition memory test for sequentially presented 320 (160 old) intermediately-sized (8.5°) images.

Participants were required to report for each image if they recall seeing it earlier (“old”) or not (“new”).

In all three experiments, data of each participant were recorded in a CSV file and this included correctness and response times for each presented image.

Indeed, perceptual performance was at ceiling for the smallest images, indicating that participants were able to understand and correctly report the content of the images they saw.

The fact that perceptual measures were at ceiling indicates that participants were easily able to perceive and extract high-level visual information from the smallest images and therefore this cannot explain why they did not remember them as well as the larger images.

Participants were instructed to either view the images (naturalistic encoding experiment) or to memorize the images (intentional memorization encoding experiment).

Ethics approval statement:

The experiments were approved by the Bar-Ilan University Interdisciplinary Studies Unit ethics committee (approval numbers ISU202007003 granted on 14.08.2020 and ISU202208002 granted on 29.08.2022) and all research was performed in accordance with the ethics committee and the Declaration of Helsinki guidelines.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
